newsitem.title: KENYA: Long drought brings ruin to Kenyan herders.
newsitem.headline: Long drought brings ruin to Kenyan herders.

text.p: Drought in northeastern Kenya is sending livestock prices plunging, bringing financial ruin and sometimes death to the region's ethnic Somali nomadic herders, whose bare bones economy relies on animals.

Not enough rain has fallen for 18 months and December short rains failed entirely, starving animals like cattle, goats and camels and sending their value plummeting until a goat costs less than a chicken.
"The local market is flooded with sub-standard cattle," said Bishar Hassan Sheikh, a trader at Wajir's livestock market.
At the same time cereal prices are rising because the drought has hit production in Kenya's agricultural heartland, only adding to the shortage of food in the dried-out north.

In Wajir district, 500 km (300 miles) northeast of Nairobi, 27.9 percent of children under the age of five were already malnourished last October and the mortality rate was 1.1 per thousand per month, according to Oxfam aid agency estimates.

"What these statistics say is we have a situation which is serious moving towards an emergency situation out of control," said Adam Leach, country director of Oxfam, the only agency operating in the northeast.
"If you don't do something now there will be an almighty crisis further down the line."
Dead animals litter the sand next to a near-empty dam at Yahut in Wajir district and at Dambas, 80 km (50 miles) north of Wajir town, cattle too weak to drink are sprawled waiting to die.
But aid workers doubt the drought in most of Kenya and other African states will as yet deeply touch a world over-fed on years-old images of starving children in Ethiopia and Somalia.
Facing general elections this year, the Kenyan government declared famine a national disaster in January, began distributing food aid and scrapped import taxes of food such as maize.
Animal herders argue they were deliberately marginalised by the government and cut off from development money as punishment for attempting to secede from Kenya at independence in 1963.
They say the state Kenya Meat Commission should build a slaughterhouse at Isiolo, a gateway town to North East Province, so the herders could sell their livestock at a better price.
It would help them little now. "The problem is our animals are worthless. They have nothing to eat and we can't eat from their value," says Hussein Nor Abdile, a Dambas herder.
"These people are vulnerable because the slightest disturbance in weather patterns has an instant impact on them," said Vincent Lelei, arid lands coordinator in the Office of the President.
